# Joshua 7: Verse-by-verse research notes

**Gaps in what I found:** I couldn't find any Joshua 7 material from the Lutheran or Orthodox sites, from wesley.nnu.edu or seedbed, from ligonier or TGC, or from bibleodyssey. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter, so those are left out. "Tradition" labels below go only on teachers the sources name. Commentators the pages leave unnamed are described as unnamed.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says the opening "But" deliberately contrasts Joshua's growing fame at the end of ch. 6 with Israel's unfaithfulness. He quotes Howard: the Hebrew word for "acted unfaithfully" is also used of a wife's adultery, so it means a betrayal of trust. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- Guzik also says the devoted things belonged to God. Taking them was theft, and denying it was deceit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- Why the whole nation is blamed: Barnes says one man's trespass is imputed to all Israel, who also share in the penalty of it. He links Achan's sacrilege to that of Ananias and Sapphira. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/7-1.htm
- Another commentator on the same page, not named in my results, says the guilt counted against the people in a civil sense, not a moral one. Achan had robbed the whole nation of the purity and holiness which it ought to possess before God, the way one limb's sin affects the whole body. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/7-1.htm
- Utley calls this "corporality": one person's act affects the whole group. He compares Adam, the sacrifices, and Christ (Rom 5). He notes the Hebrew repeats the root ("acted unfaithfully with unfaithfulness") to make the scandal stronger. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-7
- Achan's family line: Pink points out that Zerah was born from Judah's sin with Tamar (Gen 38). Precept Austin adds that Achan means "trouble." https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-7-commentary
- Constable: Achan stole what was dedicated to God, and he robbed the whole nation of its innocence before God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-7.html

**v. 2**
- Clarke identifies Ai with the "Hai" of Gen 12:8, east of Bethel and about ten or twelve miles from Jericho. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/joshua-7.html
- Precept Austin points out the contrast in the names: Beth-aven, "house of evil," next to Bethel, "house of God." It also says the name Ai means "heap of ruins." https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-7-commentary
- Madvig, quoted by Guzik, says this is the first time in the conquest that Joshua acts on his own initiative, and the text says nothing about him seeking the Lord's guidance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- **Modern scholarship (Utley):** Archeology is not sure whether Ai was settled during the time of Joshua's conquest. Utley adds that the date of the conquest is uncertain and archaeology is imprecise. He also notes that many link Ai closely with Bethel, perhaps as an outpost. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-7

**v. 3**
- Guzik says the spies' advice may have come from faith or from self-confidence. Either way, an army in disobedience could have sent 100,000 men and still lost. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- Precept Austin calls the spies' report inaccurate, since 8:25 shows Ai had at least 12,000 people. It also notes that God later told Joshua to take all the fighting men (8:1). https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-7-commentary
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: God was not with the spies to enlighten and guide them, and therefore they were deceived. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-7.html
- Utley says the Hebrew word for "thousand" can mean a literal thousand, a family unit or a military unit. He also notes the climb from Gilgal to Ai is about 3,400 feet. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-7

**v. 4**
- Precept Austin says nothing indicates Joshua asked the Lord before the battle. He prayed afterwards. It also notes the ark did not go with the troops. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-7-commentary
- Guzik quotes Maclaren: when God is driven away by sin, even Ai is not too weak to defeat Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- Matthew Henry says it was just as well only 3,000 went. Under guilt and wrath the whole army would have done no better, and the disgrace would have been worse. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_007.cfm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: 36 dead was a small number militarily, but it meant Israel *could* be defeated in the land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- Utley says the "melting heart" phrase is the one used earlier of the terrified Canaanites (2:11; 5:1). Now, because of sin, Israel feels it. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-7
- Utley says "Shebarim" probably means a quarry or ravine. He wonders whether Achan's death by stoning is a deliberate play on the chase to the stone quarry. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-7
- GotQuestions: Achan's sin led to the deaths of thirty-six of his fellow soldiers and defeat for the whole army. https://www.gotquestions.org/Achan-in-the-Bible.html

**v. 6**
- Utley lists three standard Hebrew signs of mourning: tearing clothes, putting dust on the head, and lying face down. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-7
- Guzik says they mourned the 36 men, but even more the loss of God's blessing and protection. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/

**vv. 7–8** (interpreters differ on how to judge this prayer)
- **Critical reading:** The Expositor's Bible says Joshua almost throws the blame on God. It also says he slips into the tone of the ten faithless spies he once opposed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/joshua-7.html
- Utley also sees doubt in the prayer. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-7
- Madvig, quoted by Guzik, says confidence in God's faithfulness should have made Joshua look for the cause elsewhere. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- **Kinder reading:** Clarke says the complaint came mainly from Joshua's concern for God's glory and for the people, and that some have blamed it too hastily. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/joshua-7.html
- Another source quoted by Precept Austin says the prayer seems murmuring "at first view." It also lists Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary, which calls Joshua's concern for God's honour the language of the Spirit of adoption. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-7-commentary

**v. 9**
- Matthew Henry says Joshua treats Israel's "little name" as a small loss next to God's great name. He calls this the only hopeful plea in the prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_007.cfm
- Utley: "cut off our name" is an idiom for a family line dying out completely. Pleading for God's name follows the pattern of Moses' prayers (Exod 32:12; Deut 9:28). https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-7
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: True prayer throws its principal stress on the glory of the Divine name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-7.html

**v. 10**
- Guzik quotes Schaeffer: Joshua shouldn't be on his face but out dealing with the sin among the people. Joshua didn't need to change God's heart. He needed to change Israel's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- Precept Austin quotes Vance Havner: there is a time for humble prayer, but prayer alone will not get us through. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea_devotionals

**v. 11**
- Guzik: God had not failed Israel. The whole nation is declared guilty, which he compares to "a little leaven" in 1 Cor 5:6. He quotes Howard: this shows God has no double standard between Israel and the Canaanites. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- Guzik also applies the verse to giving. Failing to give is "robbing God" (Mal 3:8), and he says New Testament giving should be regular and generous. This is his own application. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- Constable is quoted as saying the first three clauses describe the sin as an offence against God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-7.html

**v. 12**
- Guzik says believers are not under Israel's covenant of blessings and curses. A believer's standing is secure in Christ, but sin can still hinder fellowship with God and power in daily life (1 John 1:6). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- An older commentator quoted by Precept Austin: by holding on to what was cursed, Israel would transfer upon themselves the very curse denounced against their adversaries. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-7-commentary

**v. 13**
- Precept Austin: God gave Achan a night to think about his sin and repent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-7-commentary
- Guzik quotes Redpath: no Christian can sin without affecting the whole church. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- Wells of Living Water notes that Israel sanctified itself before Jordan and Jericho (3:5), but now went against Ai with sin hidden in the camp. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lwc/joshua-7.html

**v. 14**
- Clarke mentions the view that this was Urim and Thummim, but thinks it was most likely the lot. He compares Saul's selection in 1 Sam 10. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/joshua-7.html
- Guzik: sin hidden from people is never hidden from God. He quotes Trapp: even now Achan still does not confess. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/

**v. 15**
- The Believer's Study Bible, quoted by Precept Austin, says the word for "outrage" (*nevalah*) is usually used of sexual perversions. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-7-commentary
- Utley sees two punishments, stoning and then burning. He says the destruction of Achan's family and animals is another example of Hebrew corporality. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-7

**vv. 16–18**
- Guzik: it must have been agonising for Achan to watch his tribe, clan and household being picked in turn. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- The Catholic Encyclopedia says the context shows "Zabdi" and "Zerah" stand for the house and clan, not just individual ancestors. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/06408a.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says the plan to single out one man among millions supposes omniscience by its boldness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-7.html

**v. 19**
- Guzik says confessing sin gives glory to God. It acknowledges his knowledge of all things, his righteousness, his authority and his judgments. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- Utley says "give glory to the LORD" was a Hebrew idiom for telling the truth. He notes Achan confessed only after the lot exposed him. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-7

**v. 20**
- Guzik says Achan's honesty was welcome. He gave no excuses. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- Constable says confessing could not reduce Achan's punishment, but it could reduce his guilt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-7.html
- **Baptist (Adrian Rogers, via Precept Austin):** Achan wasn't glorifying God to win mercy, and he got none. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-7-commentary

**v. 21**
- Madvig, quoted by Guzik, notes that "I saw … I coveted … I took" are the same three verbs as in the Fall (Gen 3:6). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- GotQuestions cites Poole: the sin began at his eye, moved to desire, then to taking and hiding. https://www.gotquestions.org/Achan-accursed-things.html
- GotQuestions notes that Shinar was linked with Babylon's wickedness. https://www.gotquestions.org/land-of-Shinar.html
- Matthew Henry imagines Achan's excuse: it would be a pity to burn such a fine garment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_007.cfm

**vv. 22–23**
- Guzik says the careful hiding itself showed Achan knew he was guilty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- GotQuestions says the precious metals were meant for the tabernacle and so were God's property. https://www.gotquestions.org/Achan-in-the-Bible.html

**vv. 24–25: Was the family executed?** (This is the chapter's main point of disagreement.)
- **Yes, because they were complicit:**
  - Matthew Henry says most conclude the children died, and it is very probable that they assisted in the concealment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/7-25.html
  - Keil, as summarised by Coffman, says the hiding place made the family accomplices after the fact, and that God specifically commanded this execution. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/7-25.html
  - Constable makes the same complicity argument. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-7.html
  - Wiersbe, quoted by Precept Austin: since Deut 24:16 forbids punishing children for a parent's sin, the family must have been guilty of assisting him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-7-commentary
  - Fausset adds that Deut 24:16 does not apply when God himself commands the execution. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/fbd/a/achan.html
  - GotQuestions says the family were most likely complicit. It also offers a second possibility: the execution showed how pure Israel was called to be. https://www.gotquestions.org/Achan-in-the-Bible.html
- **Possibly not:**
  - **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** the children were probably brought out to watch. The text seems rather to intimate that Achan alone was stoned. He points out that the Syriac says only Achan was stoned. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/joshua-7.html
  - Guzik's commentary says the children were probably brought to watch, not executed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
  - In a later Q&A Guzik admitted his teaching had been inconsistent on this. He suggests the singular words ("him") point to Achan alone, and the plurals ("them") to his possessions. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/i-spoke-too-soon-live-qa-for-june-9-2022/
  - The ISBE, on the NET Bible's site, says the record is not explicit on these points. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=achan
  - Against this view, Precept Austin argues that "stoning" lifeless objects makes little sense, so "them" probably means the family. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-7-commentary
- **Catholic:** the Catholic Encyclopedia says Achan with his family amid herds, was stoned to death. It reads this under the law of the "anathema" (the ban). https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01455e.htm
- **Reformed (Calvin):** the whole people throwing stones showed they hated the crime and had no share in it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/7-25.html
- **Wordplay and Jewish tradition:** Utley says the rabbis took "the LORD will trouble you *this day*" to mean Achan was punished with death but did not lose eternity with God. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-7
- Howard, quoted by Guzik, says Achan in effect had become a Canaanite by his actions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- **Church Fathers:** Athanasius notes Achan didn't plead his war service as an excuse. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/2812.htm
- The Apostolic Constitutions use Achan as a warning against stealing. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/07157.htm

**v. 26**
- Calvin: the heap of stones was partly a memorial, and partly meant to stop anyone gathering gold or silver bits from the spot. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/7-25.html
- Guzik: God turned from his anger only after the judgment. Israel could then walk in God's power again. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-7/
- **The Valley of Achor as a "door of hope" (Hosea 2:15):**
  - **Baptist (Spurgeon)** preached the valley as a door of hope. He says putting sin to death brings joy to the soul. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons47/sermons47.xliii.html
  - **Reformed (Calvin on Hosea)** says Achor was the beginning of good hope for Israel's fathers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/2-15.html
  - Maclaren: first stone Achan, and then hope! https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/hosea/the-valley-of-achor.cfm
  - Bible Hub sees a picture of Christ, who bears the curse. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_was_Achan_s_family_stoned_in_Joshua_7.htm
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia notes Hosea's promise for the returning exiles and identifies the valley with Wady el-Kelt. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01103a.htm
